messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael Hernandez had always been drawn to the wilderness, finding solace in its vast expanses and rhythms. As a park ranger, he spent his days patrolling the trails, ensuring that visitors respected the land and its creatures. But it was on one of these patrols, three years ago, that Rafael's life took a devastating turn. He stumbled upon a group of poachers, who tortured him for hours, leaving him with physical scars that would never fully heal. The memories of that day haunted Rafael, refusing to cohere into a linear narrative. Some moments were seared into his mind – the sound of his own screams, the smell of sweat and blood – while others remained shrouded in darkness. When he tried to recount the event to himself or others, he found himself losing the thread, unable to finish the story. Rafael couldn't shake the feeling that his body had been permanently damaged by what happened, that he was now more vulnerable than ever before. This sense of physical vulnerability fed into a growing distrust of others. Rafael became convinced that he couldn't rely on anyone – not even his colleagues or family members – to keep him safe. He began to rehearse conversations in his head before any interaction, trying to anticipate potential threats and prepare himself for the worst. This habit soon extended beyond social interactions; Rafael found himself repeatedly checking doors and windows, convinced that something bad was waiting just outside. The fear of being caught off guard became an all-consuming threat, one that Rafael's body seemed to react to even before his mind could process it. When he encountered unexpected delays or obstacles – a slow-moving hiker on the trail, a jammed lock on his truck – Rafael's heart would start racing, his senses on high alert. He was certain that something terrible was lurking just around the corner, waiting to strike. As time passed, Rafael's behaviors became more entrenched. He began avoiding driving or being a passenger in vehicles, fearing the loss of control and potential danger. His social life suffered as well; Rafael stopped attending ranger meetings and community events, unable to shake the feeling that others would judge him or take advantage of his vulnerability. The memories of the traumatic event continued to haunt Rafael, surfacing at unexpected moments and sending him spiraling into a cycle of fear and avoidance. He numbed his feelings as best he could, trying to create distance between himself and the world around him. But this only seemed to intensify the threat; Rafael's body remained on high alert, reacting to every perceived danger with a ferocity that left him exhausted. Despite his efforts to manage these symptoms, Rafael couldn't shake the fear that he was going crazy – that his reactions since the event were evidence of some deeper psychological fracture. It was this fear that finally brought him to seek help, three years after the traumatic event. As he sat in the therapist's office, Rafael knew that he had hit rock bottom; he could no longer continue living in a state of constant vigilance and dread. "I just want to be able to walk through the woods without feeling like I'm walking into a nightmare," Rafael said, his voice barely above a whisper. "I want to trust myself again – to know that I can handle whatever comes my way."
